transcript:
# Day 13, Game Theory and Decisions: Nash equilibrium, what it is and why it is not always good (John Nash, 1928-2015; idea published 1950)

Two gas stations sit across the road from each other. Monday morning, one drops its price by five cents. By lunch the other has matched it. Tuesday, the first drops again. By Friday both are selling at almost no profit, both owners are miserable, and neither one is willing to raise prices first, because the moment he does, every car pulls into the other lot. Nobody planned this. Nobody likes it. And yet nobody will move.

That stuck place has a name. It is a Nash equilibrium, and it is the single most used idea in game theory.

The definition is short. A Nash equilibrium is a set of choices, one for each player, where no player can do better by changing their own choice alone, as long as everyone else keeps doing what they are doing. The key word is alone. It does not say the outcome is good for the group. It does not say the players are happy. It only says that each person, looking at what the others are doing, has no reason to switch. Everyone's choice is a best response to everyone else's choice, all at the same time.

Go back to the gas stations. Both at the low price: if one owner raises prices by himself, he loses his customers, so he stays. Equilibrium. Now imagine both at a high price. If one owner quietly undercuts, he grabs the whole street for a day. So high prices are not stable. Not an equilibrium. The low price outcome is the one that holds, even though both would rather be in the other one.

John Nash worked this out in his Princeton doctoral thesis in 1950, at age 21. The thesis is about 27 pages. His big contribution was not just the definition but a proof that every game with a finite number of players and choices has at least one such equilibrium, as long as you allow players to randomize between options. We will cover randomizing in a few weeks. Nash shared the 1994 Nobel memorial prize in economics for this work. A French economist, Antoine Augustin Cournot, had used the same logic for competing firms back in 1838, so the idea is older than its name, which is a pattern you will see often.

Why does this matter outside of gas stations? Because it tells you where a situation will settle if you leave it alone. An arms race between two countries is a Nash equilibrium: each side would be worse off disarming alone, so both keep spending. Two banks offering the same signup bonus. Two colleagues who both stay late because the other does. In each case the question is not "what is best for all of us" but "what will nobody walk away from." Those are different questions, and confusing them is a classic mistake.

Now the objections, and they are real. First, many games have several equilibria, and the theory does not tell you which one will happen. Second, real people often do not play the equilibrium, especially the first time. In a well known experiment, people are asked to pick a number from 0 to 100, and the winner is whoever is closest to two thirds of the average. The equilibrium is zero. Average first time guesses land around 20 to 35. Third, the theory assumes everyone is perfectly rational and knows everyone else is too. That is a tall order.

Defenders answer in two ways. Over repeated play, people and firms do tend to drift toward equilibrium as they learn, which is why the theory predicts experienced markets much better than one shot experiments. And they say Nash equilibrium was never meant as a prediction of what people do on day one. It is a consistency check: if your plan only works when the other side behaves against their own interest, it is not a plan.

One footnote worth knowing. The famous bar scene in the film A Beautiful Mind, where Nash explains his idea, actually describes an outcome that is not a Nash equilibrium. Game theorists have been grumbling about it for twenty years.

This builds directly on Day 3, where we defined players, strategies and payoffs, and on Day 8, the prisoner's dilemma. The dilemma is a special case of today's idea: an equilibrium that is bad for both players. Dominant strategies always produce a Nash equilibrium, but most real situations have no dominant strategy, and Nash's idea is what lets you analyze them anyway. There is also a real link to Sun Tzu's calculation before battle from Day 7: both ask you to assume a capable opponent who is reasoning about you.

Question for the day: pick one stuck situation at work, a standoff where nobody will move first. Is it stuck because it is bad, or because it is an equilibrium? What would have to change in someone's payoffs for them to move?

Optional source: John Nash, "Non-Cooperative Games," Annals of Mathematics, 1951, or the 1950 thesis of the same name. The definition is in the first two pages.
